mappedSpeechEvidence.text: The tube in this doctor's arm was heading toward his heart,
and the doctor pushing it forward was also the patient.
In 1929, Werner Forsman was a young physician in Eberswalde, Germany.
He wanted to reach the heart from inside a blood vessel without opening the chest.
A flexible tube could offer a way in, but his hospital director refused to let him try it on a patient.
Forsman decided to use himself.
If the experiment went wrong, the person making the discovery would also be the one paying for it.
He introduced a thin rubber catheter into a vein in his left arm and advanced it through his body.
The important part is the route. Veins carry blood back toward the heart,
so the tube could follow an existing passage instead of piercing the chest.
But being inside a vein wasn't enough. He still needed to know where the tip had gone.
With the catheter still in place, forcemen walked to the x-ray department.
His own body was carrying the experiment down the hospital corridor,
and the evidence was waiting in another room.
The x-ray supplied the answer. The catheter had reached his right atrium,
one of the heart's upper chambers. About 65 centimeters of tubing now marked a root from
his arm into his heart. He had survived, and he had a picture to prove where the tube was.
Forcemen published the experiment that November, but a startling demonstration did
not immediately become accepted medicine. His work attracted little interest,
and the surgeon Ferdinand Sauerbroek dismissed such experiments as circus work.
The picture showed what was possible. It did not persuade everyone to follow.
That took more than one man's gamble.
In the following years, Andre Cornand and Dickinson Richards developed cardiac catheterization
into a practical research method.
Doctors could sample blood and measure pressures inside the circulation,
learning how the heart and lungs worked together,
and what changed when disease struck.
In 1956, 27 years after Forseman's self-experiment,
all three men shared the Nobel Prize in medicine.
The recognition belonged to the daring first step
and the careful work that made it useful.
The tube that had once led through one doctor's arm had opened a route into the living heart.
